title: The Impact of Psychological, Economic, Social Aspects, and Interest Rate Variations on Working Millennials' Saving Patterns Through Digital Banking
authors: Ataza, C.; Porcel, M.; Resabal, L.; Sandoval, A.; Bragas, C.
tldr: A survey of 51 working millennials in Metro Manila finds that interest rate variations and psychological aspects are the strongest positive predictors of saving patterns through digital banking, while social aspects have a significant negative effect.
problem_and_motivation: Working millennials in the Philippines face a complex financial landscape shaped by psychological, economic, social, and interest rate factors when saving through digital banking platforms. Existing research lacks empirical evidence on which of these factors most significantly influence saving patterns in the Philippine digital banking context.
approach: Survey questionnaire administered via Google Forms to 51 working millennials aged 25-42 with digital bank accounts in Metro Manila, Philippines.
Purposive sampling technique selected respondents who were using digital banks and aware of saving patterns through digital banking.
Instrument adapted from Classical Theory of Interest, measuring four constructs on a 5-point Likert scale.
Cronbach's alpha reliability analysis confirmed internal consistency across all four constructs (alpha range: 0.804 to 0.926).
Multiple linear regression analysis used to assess the predictive effects of the four independent variables on saving patterns through digital banking.
Regression equation Y = b1P + b2E + b3S + b4I + c formulated and tested.
findings: num: Interest rate variations are the strongest predictor with Beta = 0.878, p < 0.001, explaining 70.06% of variance in saving behavior alone.
num: Psychological aspects positively predict saving patterns with Beta = 0.430, p = 0.006, explaining 31.02% of variance.
num: Social aspects have a significant negative effect with Beta = -0.182, p = 0.016, explaining only 8.47% of variance.
num: The combined model with all four factors explains 75.34% of the variance in saving patterns (R = 0.868).
num: Economic aspects are not statistically significant predictors (Beta = -0.130, p = 0.293) despite a moderate correlation of R = 0.514.
Social factors, despite being statistically significant, have a negative rather than positive effect on saving patterns.
The regression model Y = (0.430)P + (-0.130)E + (-0.182)S + (0.878)I + (-0.01) captures the saving pattern prediction.
84.3% of respondents were aged 26-31, aligning with PSA data showing this age group as the largest employed population segment.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This study contributes empirical evidence on the relative importance of psychological, economic, social, and interest rate factors in shaping saving behaviors among Filipino working millennials using digital banking.
directly_justifies: Interest rate variations explain 70.06% of variance in saving behavior, making it the dominant predictor.
The combined model of psychological, economic, social, and interest rate factors explains 75.34% of saving pattern variance.
Social aspects have a significant negative effect (Beta = -0.182) on saving patterns, contrary to expected positive influence.
Psychological aspects positively predict saving patterns with Beta = 0.430 at p = 0.006 significance level.
Economic aspects are not statistically significant predictors (p = 0.293) despite moderate individual correlation.
limits: Small sample size of 51 respondents limits generalizability to the broader Filipino millennial population.
Purposive sampling may introduce selection bias as respondents were self-selected digital banking users.
Cross-sectional survey design captures only a snapshot, preventing causal inference about temporal relationships.
No control for confounding variables such as financial literacy level, total assets, or household size.
Economic aspects not being significant may reflect measurement limitations rather than true non-influence.

remember_this: Interest rate variations explain 70.06% of variance in saving patterns, making it the dominant predictor among all factors tested.
Social aspects have a statistically significant negative effect on saving behavior, contrary to conventional expectations.
The combined regression model explains 75.34% of saving pattern variance across four predictor variables.
Psychological factors positively influence saving patterns, supporting the role of self-efficacy and financial confidence.
The study uses a small purposive sample of 51 Metro Manila millennials, limiting generalizability.
